root.note: One of the best-known Indo-European words: Latin bōs, Greek boûs and Sanskrit gáuḥ come from it too.

stages.meaning: a big farm animal that gives milk

history: Cow comes from Old English cū. Its old plural was cȳ, later kine, which you may still meet in old books and the Bible. For the meat, English uses a different word: beef. After the Norman Conquest of 1066, the new rulers of England spoke French. The English farmers kept the animals and their English names: cow, calf, sheep, swine. The meat on the tables of the French-speaking lords got French names: beef (boef), veal (veel), mutton (moton) and pork (porc). Historians say the real story is a bit more complicated, but the pairs are still in English today. The funny part: cow and beef are distant relatives. Both go back to the same Indo-European word for cattle.
historyEinfach: Cow is an old English word. The meat of a cow is beef. Why two words? In 1066, French-speaking people came to England. They were the rich people. English farmers looked after the cows. The rich people ate the meat, and they used French words: beef, pork. So the animal has an English name, and the meat has a French name.

synonyms.note: cows and bulls as a group; always plural

cognates.note: from Old French boef, from Latin bōs: a distant relative

elsewhere.text: French bœuf (‘ox, beef’) is where English beef comes from. Through Latin bōs it goes back to the same old root as cow, so the animal and its meat are distant cousins.
German Kuh is a close sister of cow. German also has the old irregular plural: Kühe, with a changed vowel, like Old English cȳ.
